analysis.one_liner: Funds housing and services for homeless people with new taxes on luxury real estate and big landlords.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to five House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create and expand federal programs for people who are homeless or at risk of losing housing: new block grants for affordable housing and basic infrastructure like public bathrooms, mobile crisis teams as an alternative to police response, expanded emergency food and shelter grants, and help voting for people without a fixed address. It would stop federal money from going to cities that arrest people for sleeping outside, and pay for all of it with new taxes on high-end real estate sales, property deals hidden behind anonymous companies, and large corporate landlords.
analysis.who_benefits: People experiencing homelessness or housing instability, households spending too much of their income on rent, and the local governments and nonprofits that serve them. The bill defines 'housing-unstable' broadly, including people paying over a fifth of their income on rent, people exiting jail or detention, and domestic violence survivors. It would also fund permanent affordable housing for people earning 30% or less of area median income.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Community Development Block Grant Plus program that can fund construction of permanently affordable housing, public bathrooms and water fountains, and housing services, with at least $6 billion authorized annually [S2][S3].

Authorizes $100 million a year for alternatives to arresting homeless people, including pre-arrest diversion programs and mobile crisis teams staffed by health professionals instead of law enforcement [S3].

Bars federal assistance to any government that criminally punishes homeless people for sleeping outside or disposes of their belongings without due process, and withholds matching-fund requirements from jurisdictions that commit to a Housing First approach [S2][S3].

Authorizes roughly $10 billion each for the emergency solutions grant and continuum of care programs, plus $1 billion for FEMA emergency food and shelter grants, expanding eligible uses to hygiene, tiny-home shelters, and medical respite housing [S3].

Directs a study of state laws that keep homeless and housing-unstable people from voting and funds nonprofits to help them vote, and lets homeless representatives get surplus federal buildings by deed on an expedited basis [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sellers and buyers of $10 million-plus real estate (a 5% tax split between them), transfers involving companies whose true owners are hidden from public records (10%), and corporate landlords owning large numbers of rental units (1% of rent), who could avoid the tax by accepting rent control, just-cause eviction, or source-of-income protections. General taxpayers would cover any gap between the tax revenue and the authorized spending.
analysis.who_pays_short: Luxury real estate parties and big landlords

drawbacks.text: The new taxes would raise the cost of large real estate transactions and of renting from large corporate landlords; some of the rental tax could be passed through or push landlords to restructure holdings below the ownership thresholds to avoid it [S3].
The bill authorizes roughly $27 billion a year and conditions most spending on revenue from the new taxes that may fall short, leaving general appropriations to fill the gap [S3].

Making federal funds conditional on jurisdictions not enforcing bans on public camping would leave cities that rely on those laws without new assistance, which critics argue limits flexibility for local governments managing encampments [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and targeted at one of the country's most acute problems: hundreds of thousands of unsheltered people, services for them, and permanent housing for the lowest-income households. The costs fall almost entirely on high-value property transactions and large corporate landlords rather than ordinary homeowners or small landlords, though the new taxes could discourage some high-end sales and the funding structure depends on revenue that may not materialize. The bill's chief weakness is political, not design: its scale and its penalty on jurisdictions that criminalize camping made it a heavy lift in a narrowly divided Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees on the day it was introduced and, aside from one subcommittee referral 21 months later, no committee ever took it up, so it never reached the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on March 22, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the Financial Services, House Administration, Judiciary, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means committees [S1][S5].
Twenty-nine House Democrats joined as cosponsors; no Republican did [S4].
The only further action in two years was a referral to the Financial Services Subcommittee on Work and Welfare on December 17, 2024, less than three weeks before the Congress ended [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large landlords, high-end real estate buyers and sellers, and owners who hold property behind anonymous companies avoided the new taxes, and no jurisdiction faced the bill's conditions on how it treats homeless people. People experiencing homelessness gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big landlords and luxury property owners

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its advocacy

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee to which the bill was primarily referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the two years it was pending; the only action was a late subcommittee referral in December 2024

against.name: House Ways and Means, Judiciary, Education and the Workforce, and House Administration Committees
against.role: Other committees to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill's provisions within their jurisdiction

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling committee schedules and the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Allowed the bill to sit without consideration for the remainder of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 30 original supporters in the House were Democrats — the sponsor plus 29 cosponsors — and the record shows no Republican support or opposition activity.

industries.note: A 1% tax on rent from landlords with 1,000+ units in one metro area, 2,000+ units overall, or 500+ across three states, waived for units under rent control, just-cause eviction, or source-of-income protections — effectively a financial incentive to accept tenant protections. The bill died, so these landlords keep paying no such tax.
A 5% tax on property sales of $10 million or more, split between buyer and seller, to fund homeless programs. Never enacted, so high-end transactions remain untaxed at the federal level.

industries.industry: Buyers and sellers using anonymous entities
industries.note: A 10% tax on property transfers involving entities whose beneficial owners are not in freely accessible public records, with an escape hatch for participants in the legal entity identifier program. It would have made hiding ownership behind shell companies costly; it never took effect.

industries.industry: Nonprofit homeless service and housing providers
industries.note: The bill's funding would flow largely to governments and nonprofits for shelters, services, and affordable housing construction. Nothing was enacted, so they continue to compete for existing, smaller funding streams.
